draft.title: Rights of suspects
card: A suspect is a person police believe may have committed an offence. The law gives suspects rights so police cannot treat them unfairly.
On arrest, a person must be told that they are under arrest and why. Police must also caution them, which means warning them that they do not have to say anything.
A detained suspect can contact a lawyer and have a lawyer advise them before questioning. Police must also give a suspect who is detained for questioning a reasonable chance to do so.

The right to silence means a suspect does not have to answer police questions. It has limits in NSW: in some cases a court may draw an unfavourable inference from silence, and a person must still give their name and address in certain situations.
draft.remember: Suspects have rights that protect them from unfair treatment, but the right to silence is not absolute.

a.q: Which right is a suspect given when arrested?
opts: To be told that they are arrested and why
To choose which police officer questions them
To leave once they have been charged
To see all the evidence police hold against them
a.why: A person who is arrested must be told that they are under arrest and the reason. The card does not give suspects a choice of officer or a right to all the evidence. Being charged does not mean they are free to leave.
a.clue: Think about what police must say at the moment of arrest.

b.q: Dev is questioned by police about a break-in and stays silent. At his trial, a court draws an unfavourable inference from this. What does this show about the right to silence?
opts: It has limits in NSW, so silence can count against a suspect
It does not exist in NSW, so suspects must answer questions
It applies only after trial, so police can demand answers
It is absolute, so silence can never be mentioned in court
b.why: The right to silence means a suspect does not have to answer, but in NSW it has limits. A court may in some cases draw an unfavourable inference from silence. It is wrong to say the right is absolute or does not exist, because suspects are still not forced to answer.
b.clue: The right exists, but the card says it has limits.

a.best: To be told that they are arrested and why

b.best: It has limits in NSW, so silence can count against a suspect

problems.detail: The card says police must caution a person 'on arrest'. Under NSW LEPRA (s 122), the caution must be given before questioning or an investigative procedure begins, not necessarily at the moment of arrest. Wording such as 'Before questioning, police must caution them' would be more accurate.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear correct answer that matches the card and NSW law. One small fact needs fixing: in NSW the caution must be given before questioning, not strictly at the moment of arrest.
